name: 7-Toed Pete (Dominoes Variant)
description: Seven-Toed Pete is a connecting domino game in the Fives family played with a double-six set. Four players build a cross-shaped layout from a single spinner, scoring whenever the open ends total a multiple of five and taking extra turns for scoring plays or doubles.

overview.description: Seven-Toed Pete is a connecting domino game in the Fives family played with a double-six set. Four players build a cross-shaped layout from a single spinner, scoring whenever the open ends total a multiple of five and taking extra turns for scoring plays or doubles.

history.origins: Seven-Toed Pete is an American domino game in the Fives family, using a double-six set and scoring on multiples of five.
timeline: Modern era: documented as a Fives-family domino game credited to Joe Celko and John McLeod.
history.cultural: A fast-paced social domino game played in the USA; the name Seven-Toed Pete is also used as an alternative name for Seven-Card Stud poker, though the two games are otherwise unrelated.
history.evolution: Regional rules distinguish an East Coast version, where only the first double played is a spinner, from a West Coast version in which all doubles are spinners and the game is often called Race Horse or Horse Race.

setup.players: Four players in the basic game; two or three players can play a draw variant with a boneyard.
setup.dealing: For four players, each receives seven tiles and there is no boneyard. For two or three players, each receives seven tiles and the remaining tiles form a boneyard to draw from when unable to play.
setup.equipment: Double-six domino set, scoring chips or markers

rules.objective: Score points by making the open ends of the layout total a multiple of five and by winning hands with the lowest pip total; the first player to reach the agreed total of points or chips wins.
rules.gameplay: The game uses a double-six domino set. Each player receives seven tiles. In the four-player game there is no boneyard; in the two- or three-player variant, remaining tiles form a boneyard to draw from when a player cannot play. The first scoring tile or double led starts the layout, and the first double played becomes the only spinner, from which four arms of a cross-shaped layout grow. Players in turn match the open ends; whenever a player makes the open ends total a multiple of five or plays a double, that player takes an immediate extra turn. If a player cannot play and there is a boneyard, they must draw until able to play; otherwise they pass. A hand ends when a player dominoes with their last tile or when the game is blocked with no legal plays.
keyRules: Member of the Fives family of domino games; scoring on multiples of five.
Uses a double-six domino set and usually four players, each taking seven tiles.
Only the first double played becomes the spinner, producing a four-armed cross layout.
Playing a double or making the open ends total a multiple of five grants an extra turn.
A hand ends when a player dominoes or the game is blocked; the winner scores from opponents' remaining tiles.

strategy.basic: Keep flexible tiles that match common end values and avoid being stuck without a legal play, while looking for chances to score multiples of five.
strategy.intermediate: Plan sequences that let you chain scoring plays or doubles to take multiple turns in a row and reduce your pip total before the layout becomes tight.
strategy.advanced: Track which high-pip tiles and key scoring combinations are still unplayed so you can steer the layout ends to values that are awkward for opponents but favorable to your remaining tiles.

scoring.description: Whenever a player makes the open ends of the layout total a multiple of five, they score that total; the winner of the hand (the player who dominoes or has the fewest pips when the game blocks) scores the total pip value of opponents' remaining tiles, often divided by five into points or chips.
scoring.winCondition: Play continues over multiple hands, and the first player to reach the agreed total of points or chips wins.
